  2. Schematic Design — 15% fee; conceptual design
  3. Design Development — 20% fee; detailed design
  4. Contract Documents — 50% fee; construction docs
  5. Bidding/Negotiation — 5% fee; contractor selection
  6. Construction Admin. — 10% fee; site visits
 SPP Documents 201–209 establish standards for architectural services scope, fee structures, and professional responsibilities under RA 9266. Fee distribution: SD=15%, DD=20%, CD=50%, BA=5%, CA=10%. Contract Documents (50%) is the largest phase. Cumulative: 15%→35%→85%→90%→100%. --- ## Related Articles - [SPP Doc 202 Six-Phase Framework](lea-prac-svc-004) - [Schematic Design Phase](lea-prac-svc-005) - [Design Development Phase](lea-prac-svc-006) - [Contract Documents Phase](lea-prac-svc-007) - [Bidding and Construction Admin](lea-prac-svc-008) - [Pre-Design Services](lea-prac-svc-001) - [Specialized Services](lea-prac-svc-009) - [Design-Build Delivery](lea-prac-svc-019) - [Fee Compensation Methods](lea-prac-cmp-001) - [Owner-Architect Agreement](lea-prac-ctr-001)

rows.title: CPD Requirements for Architects
rows.content:
## CPD Requirements for Architects

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- State the CPD requirements for architects: total CPD credit units per renewal period.
- Explain the CPD renewal cycle and how it aligns with PRC ID renewal.
- Describe the consequences of non-compliance with CPD requirements.
- Identify the CPD Council's role in accrediting CPD programs.

### Mandate and Regulatory Framework
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-prac-frm-008-cpd-requirements-for-ar" type="image" caption="CPD Credit Distribution — Five Professional Track Areas" description="Pie chart and bar graph showing the five CPD professional track categories: (1) Technical and Engineering Subjects — structural, materials, utilities, design; (2) Ethics and Professional Practice — code of conduct, RA 9266, SPP documents; (3) Management and Business — practice management, project management, finance; (4) Environmental and Social Responsibility — sustainability, accessibility, heritage; (5) Specialized or Emerging Topics — BIM, data privacy, green building. Each track shown with minimum credit allocation and example activity types." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-prac-frm-008-cpd-requirements-for-ar" type="image" caption="CPD Requirements Summary — Credit Units, Renewal Cycle, and Compliance" description="Summary infographic showing: (1) 45 credit units required every 3 years (average 15/year); (2) Three-year renewal cycle aligned with PRC ID renewal; (3) Distribution across 5 professional track areas with minimum credit allocations for each; (4) Timeline: RA 10912 effective August 2016, mandatory for PIC renewal from July 2017; (5) Consequences of non-compliance: PIC renewal denial, cannot legally practice, sign/seal documents, or execute professional services. Key metrics highlighted: 45 credits, 3 years, 5 tracks." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

RA 10912, the Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Act of 2016, establishes mandatory CPD requirements for all practicing architects to maintain professional licensure. The law took effect on 16 August 2016, making CPD compliance essential for PRC Professional Identification Card (PIC) renewal starting 1 July 2017. The Board of Architecture prescribes CPD guidelines in consultation with the integrated and accredited professional organization of architects.

CPD requirements apply uniformly to all registered architects maintaining active professional practice in the Philippines. Architects retiring from practice or holding inactive licenses are not required to complete CPD. The Board determines specific credit requirements, activity types, and provider accreditation standards. These guidelines establish levels of compliance and proficiency evaluation as rating factors. Architects must understand that CPD is mandatory for professional ID card renewal and active practice authorization.

### Credit Units and Compliance Cycle

Architects must accumulate 45 credit units every three years to renew their PRC Professional Identification Card. The three-year cycle establishes the compliance period; architects track completion between renewal dates. Credit units are awarded for various professional activities, ranging from structured courses offering higher credits to self-directed learning providing modest credits. Architects must distribute their CPD across multiple activity types to ensure balanced professional development covering multiple knowledge areas.

<ExamTip>Memorize these CPD numbers: 45 credits every 3 years (average 15/year), distributed across 5 professional track areas. No annual minimum is mandated — you may complete requirements unevenly as long as the three-year total is achieved. Failure = PIC renewal denial.</ExamTip>

The 45-unit requirement over three years averages 15 units annually, though no annual minimum is mandated; architects may complete requirements unevenly as long as the three-year total is achieved. Documentation requirements include course certificates, attendance records, or completion proofs from accredited providers. Architects must maintain records of all CPD activities and provide evidence upon PRC request during ID card renewal. Failure to meet the 45-unit requirement results in PIC renewal denial until requirements are satisfied.

### Distribution Across Five Professional Track Areas

CPD activities fall within five major professional track categories, with minimum credit allocations specified for each area. These tracks ensure comprehensive professional development across diverse knowledge domains. Track categories typically include technical and engineering subjects, ethics and professional practice, management and business, environmental and social responsibility, and specialized or emerging topics. Each track requires minimum credits to prevent concentration in narrow specializations.

Architects must plan their CPD portfolio to ensure compliance with distribution requirements across all five tracks. This structure prevents narrow focus on preferred subjects while neglecting essential professional competencies. A course covering multiple track areas may award credits in each applicable category, allowing flexible portfolio construction. The Board publishes guidelines specifying credit allocation for each approved activity type within each track category. Architects must verify that their selected CPD activities appropriately distribute credits across required categories.

### PRC ID Renewal Process and Timeline

PIC renewal occurs every three years, with renewal periods determined by the PRC based on registration date. Architects must submit renewal applications including proof of CPD completion before their current ID expires. The application requires evidence of all CPD activities and credit hours claimed. The Board or PRC verifies documentation and confirms CPD compliance before issuing renewal authorization. Failure to complete requirements before renewal date results in the ID becoming inactive until compliance is demonstrated.

The renewal process includes paying prescribed annual registration fees for the three-year period. Architects may renew online through the PRC system or submit applications in person at the PRC office. Fee payment and CPD documentation must be submitted together to complete renewal. Processing typically requires several weeks; architects should initiate renewal procedures well in advance of expiration dates. The renewed PIC bears a new expiration date three years in the future and confirms current registration status and continued practice authorization.

### Impact on Professional Practice Authorization

Active PIC status directly enables legal architectural practice in the Philippines. An architect without a valid, renewed PIC cannot legally practice architecture, sign and seal architectural documents, or execute professional services. Architects employed by firms or government agencies cannot practice architecture without current PIC status, regardless of employment status. This universal requirement ensures all practicing architects meet CPD standards and maintain current professional knowledge.

<Tip>An architect without a valid, renewed PIC CANNOT legally practice architecture, sign and seal documents, or execute professional services — regardless of employment status. Expired PIC = no practice authorization. Maintain current CPD completion to avoid interruption.</Tip>

Architects with expired PIC renewal can restore active status by completing outstanding CPD requirements and submitting renewal documentation. The restoration process reactivates the PIC effective upon approval, but projects undertaken during the lapsed period may be questioned regarding professional authority. Clients may refuse to accept services from architects without valid PIC status, and government agencies cannot employ non-licensed architects for architectural work. Maintaining current PIC status through timely CPD completion is essential for uninterrupted professional practice.

---

rows.title: Schedule of Payments Phase Percentages
rows.content:
## Schedule of Payments — Phase Percentages and the Architect's Invoicing Timeline

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Describe the schedule of payments per SPP Doc 202 phase.
- Identify phase percentages: SD (20%), DD (20%), CD (30%), Bidding (5%), CA (25%).
- Explain the architect's invoicing timeline tied to phase completion.
- Apply payment schedule rules to fee computation scenarios.

---
### The Five Design Phases and Payment Allocation

The SPP 202 standard Schedule of Payments divides the total architect fee across five phases aligned with project progression: Acceptance/Mobilization (5% upon contract signing), Schematic Design (20% cumulative of total fee), Design Development (40% cumulative of total fee), Contract Documents (90% cumulative of total fee), Bidding Assistance (95% cumulative of total fee), and Construction Administration (100% cumulative of total fee). These percentages reflect the typical effort distribution across a Design-Bid-Build delivery method and apply consistently to both percentage-of-cost and MDPE compensation methods.

### Schematic Design Phase Payment (15%)

Schematic Design encompasses the architect's initial design exploration and development. The architect meets with the client to understand objectives, develops preliminary design concepts, evaluates site and program requirements, explores spatial organization and design directions, and presents design concepts for client approval. This phase typically culminates in schematic designs showing the design direction, general layouts, and preliminary spatial planning. The architect receives 5% acceptance fee upon signing of the agreement, and an additional 15% upon completion of Schematic Design and client approval of the design direction, for a cumulative total of 20% of the professional fee.

### Design Development Phase Payment (20%)

Design Development refines the approved schematic design into more detailed drawings. The architect develops floor plans, elevations, building sections, and details; coordinates structural and MEP systems preliminary layouts; refines building dimensions and proportions; develops cost estimates and finalize PCC; and prepares Design Development documents for client review. This phase culminates in Design Development documents sufficient for cost estimation and client approval. The architect receives an additional 20% of total fee upon completion of Design Development documents and client approval of design refinement, bringing the cumulative total to 40% of the professional fee.

### Contract Documents Phase Payment (50%)

Contract Documents represent the most effort-intensive phase. The architect prepares detailed construction documents including final floor plans, elevations, sections, detailed drawings, specifications, and general conditions notes. The architect coordinates final structural and MEP system designs with consultants, develops detailed specifications for all building systems, prepares large-scale details, addresses constructability and cost efficiency, and responds to consultant review comments. This phase culminates in documents complete and ready for public bidding (in Design-Bid-Build) or contractor submission. The architect receives an additional 50% of total fee upon completion of Contract Documents ready for bidding or construction, bringing the cumulative total to 90% of the professional fee.

### Bidding Assistance Phase Payment (5%)

<LawCallout code="uap" section="SPP Doc. 202 - Schedule of Payments">
RA 9266, Section 22 — Architect's compensation based on percentage of construction cost or other agreed basis.
</LawCallout>
Bidding Assistance covers the architect's support during contractor selection. The architect clarifies document ambiguities for bidders, prepares addenda addressing questions, issues addenda as needed, manages the document distribution process, and attends the bid opening. This phase may include a brief period of project manual preparation. The architect receives an additional 5% of total fee upon completion of bidding and contract award, bringing the cumulative total to 95% of the professional fee. (or in some formats, upon client approval to proceed to Construction Administration).

### Construction Administration Phase Payment (10%)

Construction Administration encompasses on-site observation, coordination, documentation, and certification. The architect observes construction progress, verifies that work conforms to Contract Documents, reviews requests for information and shop drawings, authorizes change orders when appropriate, maintains project schedules and payment records, and certifies substantial and final completion. This phase extends from construction start through final completion and architect sign-off on the project. The architect typically receives the remaining 5% of total fee upon substantial completion, with final payment upon final completion and close-out of all outstanding items, bringing the total to 100% of the professional fee.

### Payment Invoice Timing and Procedures

The architect typically submits invoices following completion of each phase and client approval of phase deliverables. Invoicing procedures should be established in the contract, specifying invoice format, documentation requirements, and payment terms (net 30 days is standard). The architect should document completion of each phase through client approval signatures or written approvals, creating clear basis for invoice submission.

### Variations in Payment Schedules

While the standard SPP 202 cumulative percentages (5-20-40-90-95-100) apply to most Design-Bid-Build projects, alternative delivery methods may justify different allocations. Design-Build and CM at Risk projects often front-load payments to earlier phases due to compressed schedules and early contractor involvement. Projects with extensive pre-design planning, site investigation, or feasibility studies may establish additional early-phase payments. Limited-scope projects (partial services) may consolidate or eliminate phases. The contract should specify which payment schedule applies.

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Given a project budget, determine the architect's fee. Common scenario: PCC = Php 10M × 12% fee = Php 1.2M. Watch for distractors that include land cost or architect's fee in the PCC calculation.</ExamTip>
### Milestone-Based vs. Time-Based Billing

SPP 202 payment schedules are milestone-based, tied to phase completion and client approval. This differs from time-based billing where the architect invoices periodically (monthly) based on effort expended. Milestone-based schedules better protect the architect by creating clear payment triggers; they also benefit clients by establishing transparent payment expectations. Mixing milestone-based and time-based elements requires clear contract specification.

### Holdback and Lien Waivers

Some owners retain a percentage of each payment (typically 5–10%) as security until project completion. This holdback is released upon final completion. The architect should negotiate whether holdback applies and if so, what percentage and conditions. Lien waivers may be required at each payment milestone; the architect should clarify whether conditional lien waivers (protecting future work) or unconditional waivers are required.

### Payment Schedule Modifications for Extended Projects

Projects extending beyond initial estimates require clear contract provisions regarding payment timing. If Construction Administration extends significantly beyond 12–24 months, the contract should specify whether additional compensation applies or whether the 10% Construction Administration fee covers extended administration. Similarly, if Design phase approval cycles extend, the contract should address whether additional compensation applies for extended Design Development or Contract Documents phases.

### Schedule of Payments in Contract Documentation

<KeyValues pairs={[["PCC Inclusions", "Labor, materials, equipment, contractor overhead and profit"], ["PCC Exclusions", "Architect's fee, land cost, contingency, legal fees"], ["Typical Fee", "10–15% of PCC depending on project complexity"]]} />

The Schedule of Payments should be clearly documented in the Owner-Architect Agreement, specifying percentages for each phase, invoice timing, payment terms, any holdback provisions, and lien waiver requirements. A well-specified payment schedule protects both parties by establishing clear expectations regarding compensation and cash flow timing.

---

Shows cumulative fee progression and typical billing milestones at each phase completion." />

rows.content:
## Pre-Design Services: Scope, Deliverables, and Compensation Method
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

- Define pre-design services under SPP Doc 201 and explain how they differ from regular design phases.
- Identify the scope and deliverables of pre-design services: problem identification, site analysis, and initial conceptualization.
- Describe the compensation methods for pre-design services (lump sum, professional fee plus overhead, per diem).
- Apply pre-design service classifications to LEA scenarios involving early-stage architectural engagements.

SPP Document 201 defines pre-design services as the architectural work performed before the architect begins regular design phases. These services range from initial problem identification through activities that allow the architect to initially conceptualize architectural and allied solutions.

<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-prac-svc-001-pre-design-services-sco" type="image" caption="Pre-Design Services Workflow — From Consultation to Concept" description="Workflow chart showing the pre-design service sequence: consultation → pre-feasibility studies → feasibility studies → site selection/analysis → architectural programming → space planning → design brief preparation → value management → project definition. Based on SPP Doc 201." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

### What Constitutes Pre-Design Services

<KeyValues pairs={[["SPP Document", "201 (Pre-Design), 202 (Regular Design), 203 (Specialized)"], ["Compensation", "MDPE, Lump Sum, Per Diem, Professional Fee + Expenses"], ["Fee Basis", "Percentage of PCC or MDPE"]]} />
Pre-design services cover a broad line of architectural services starting from consultation to activities supporting initial project conceptualization. They include consultation, pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, site selection and analysis, site utilization and land-use studies, architectural research, architectural programming, space planning, space management studies, value management, design brief preparation, and promotional services. The architect typically prepares a proposal or contract with the client outlining the scope of work, manner of payment, owner's responsibilities, and other conditions before commencing pre-design services.

### Key Deliverables in Pre-Design Work

<KeyValues pairs={[["SPP Document", "201 (Pre-Design), 202 (Regular Design), 203 (Specialized)"], ["Compensation", "MDPE, Lump Sum, Per Diem, Professional Fee + Expenses"], ["Fee Basis", "Percentage of PCC or MDPE"]]} />

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Expect scenario-based questions where you must determine which phase a specific deliverable belongs to. Key percentages to memorize: Schematic Design (15%), Design Development (35%), Contract Documents (50%).</ExamTip>
The architect's pre-design deliverables depend on the service type but typically include analysis documents, feasibility reports, space programs, site studies, and design briefs. Consultation services produce written advice and direction on contemplated projects. Pre-feasibility studies involve procurement and analysis of secondary information to aid early decision-making. Feasibility studies provide detailed analysis determining the viability of a proposed development.

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Expect scenario-based questions where you must determine which phase a specific deliverable belongs to. Key percentages to memorize: Schematic Design (15%), Design Development (35%), Contract Documents (50%).</ExamTip>
### Compensation Methods for Pre-Design Services

<LawCallout code="uap" section="SPP Doc. 201 - Pre-Design Services">
Process flow: Identify needs → Define scope → Prepare proposal → Execute activities → Deliver outputs → Owner approval
</LawCallout>

<ProcessFlow steps={["Identify client needs", "Define scope of services", "Prepare proposal/contract", "Execute pre-design activities", "Deliver phase outputs", "Submit for owner approval"]} />

SPP 201 establishes that compensation for pre-design services may be based on one or more methods. One compensation method is Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses (MDPE), a cost-based approach that may be applied to certain pre-design activities. The multiplier ranges from 1.5 to 2.5 depending on office set-up, overhead, and architect experience. Other compensation methods include professional fee plus expenses, lump sum or fixed fee, and per diem plus reimbursable expenses for specialized personal time activities.

---

rows.title: Lump Sum Fixed Fee Scope Discipline Risk Allocation
rows.content:
## Lump Sum Fixed Fee — Scope Discipline, Risk Allocation, and Appropriate Use

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define lump sum or fixed fee compensation.
- Explain the scope, discipline, and risk allocation of a fixed fee.
- Identify when a lump sum fee is appropriate vs. risky.
- Distinguish lump sum from percentage-of-PCC and MDPE.

---
### Definition and Characteristics of Lump Sum Fixed Fee

A Lump Sum Fixed Fee is a single, predetermined amount for all design services from Schematic Design through Construction Administration. The fee does not increase if the architect works additional hours, implements scope expansion, or responds to client changes. Conversely, the fee does not decrease if the architect completes the project more efficiently than estimated. Lump sum fees are attractive to clients because they provide budget certainty and eliminate surprise invoicing; they are risky for architects because they transfer cost risk.

### Appropriate Uses of Lump Sum Fixed Fee

Lump sum fees are appropriate for projects with clearly defined, stable scope where the architect has extensive experience and high confidence in estimating effort. Straightforward residential projects where the architect has completed similar projects are candidates for lump sum fees. Small, standardized commercial buildings with conventional systems may justify lump sum compensation if scope is crystal clear.

Lump sum fees work best when the client's program is fixed and approved, when the site is well-understood, when building systems are conventional and predictable, and when the architect has completed similar projects recently. Renovation projects may justify lump sum fees if existing conditions are fully documented and understood before design begins.

Lump sum fees are also appropriate when the architect has internal efficiency advantages that allow cost recovery at a negotiated fixed price below what competitors would charge. This requires confidence that the firm can deliver quality services within the estimated scope without loss.

### Inappropriate Uses of Lump Sum Fixed Fee

<ExamTip>
  **LEA Priority — Fee Computation:** Know the five compensation methods (percentage-of-PCC, MDPE, lump sum, per diem/retainer, reimbursable expenses). Master the sliding scale for Groups 1-3 (5%→4%→3%→2%→1% for successive ₱50M brackets). Remember: DAEDS = all disciplines; DADS ≈ 60% of DAEDS (architecture only). Group 9 renovation = 150% of base group rate.
</ExamTip>

<LawCallout code="irr" section="Architect's Guidelines / SPP 202" title="Fee Computation — Regulatory Basis">
Fee computation under the Architect's Guidelines follows SPP 202 classification groups and the DAEDS/DADS framework. The percentage-of-PCC method applies group-specific rates to Project Construction Cost. MDPE uses direct personnel expense multiplied by an agreed factor. Lump-sum fees are negotiated based on scope. All methods must be documented in the owner-architect agreement.
</LawCallout>

<KeyValues items=[{"value": "5-12%", "label": "DAEDS Fee Range"}, {"value": "50M", "label": "PCC Bracket Threshold"}, {"value": "10 Groups", "label": "Project Classification"}, {"value": "150%", "label": "Renovation Multiplier"}] />
Lump sum fees are highly risky for projects with uncertain scope, innovative design, emerging programs, or complex site conditions. Projects involving significant pre-design work (programming, feasibility analysis) should not use lump sum fees because scope is not adequately defined. Design-Build or CM at Risk projects with evolving scope are unsuitable for lump sum architect fees because the architect's scope changes as the project develops.

Lump sum fees are inappropriate for projects with constrained timelines, demanding regulatory environments, or complex stakeholder coordination where scope creep is predictable. Projects with client uncertainty about program or aesthetics should avoid lump sum fees; the inevitable design revisions and refinements will exhaust the architect's fee.

### Establishing Appropriate Lump Sum Fees

To establish lump sum fees, the architect must: (1) completely understand the project scope and create detailed scope documentation; (2) estimate the effort required at each phase (Schematic Design, Design Development, Contract Documents, Bidding Assistance, Construction Administration); (3) apply standard phase percentages (15–20–50–5–10) to understand effort distribution; (4) calculate fully-loaded hourly costs for expected team composition; (5) multiply hours by hourly costs to estimate effort cost; (6) apply overhead and profit multiplier; and (7) add contingency.

Example: A straightforward small office building scope is clearly defined. Estimated effort is 800 design hours plus 200 coordination hours. Average fully-loaded hourly cost is 500 pesos per hour. Base effort cost is 1,000 × 500 = 500,000 pesos. Applying 2.2 multiplier (overhead and profit) yields 1.1 million pesos. Adding 15% contingency for scope variations yields final lump sum of 1.265 million pesos.

### Scope Definition and Lump Sum Certainty

Lump sum fees require exceptionally detailed scope documentation. The Owner-Architect Agreement must specify: what deliverables the architect will provide (specific drawing sets, specifications, schedules), what coordination the architect will perform with consultants (will the architect coordinate MEP and structural, or only document consultant work?), how many design review cycles the client receives before issuing Contract Documents, what revisions the architect will make based on client comments, what happens if the client changes the program or aesthetics after Schematic Design approval, and what constitutes the end of each phase.

Without clear scope documentation, the architect faces scope creep: unwritten expectations that the architect will provide additional services beyond the fee scope. The client believes certain services are included; the architect believes they are excluded. The architect must invest additional uncompensated hours or refuse to provide services, damaging the client relationship.

### Contingency and Risk Management in Lump Sum Fees

Even with clear scope, unexpected conditions arise. The architect should include contingency—typically 10–20%—in the lump sum fee to cover minor scope variations, additional client review cycles, or unexpected coordination requirements. Projects with higher uncertainty or greater interaction complexity should apply larger contingencies (15–20%). Straightforward projects with minimal uncertainty may apply smaller contingencies (10–15%).

The contingency belongs to the architect to cover variations within the scope. If the project requires work materially beyond the scope definition (such as significant program changes, extensive regulatory revisions, or major schedule delays), the architect should invoke the contract's scope change provision and invoice additional fees.

### Lump Sum vs. Percentage-of-PCC and MDPE Comparison

Lump sum fees are highest-risk for the architect but provide greatest budget certainty for the client. Percentage-of-PCC shares risk between architect and client: if construction costs increase, architect fee increases proportionally. MDPE shares risk through hourly accounting: if the project requires more hours, the architect bills additional hours (if not capped). Lump sum places all risk on the architect: the fee does not adjust regardless of hours or costs.

For equivalent projects, lump sum fees should be lower than MDPE or percentage-of-PCC to reflect the architect's assumption of scope and cost risk. If the architect estimates 1.5 million pesos MDPE fee, the lump sum fee should be 10–20% lower (1.2–1.35 million) to reflect risk transfer.

### Payment Structure for Lump Sum Fees

Lump sum fees should still follow standard phase percentages for invoicing: 15% at Schematic Design completion, 20% at Design Development completion, 50% at Contract Documents completion, 5% at Bidding completion, 10% at Construction Administration completion. This structure ensures the architect receives payment as milestones are achieved rather than invoicing the entire fee in advance or at project completion.

Some lump sum contracts establish monthly or periodic invoicing based on estimated completion percentage of work. The contract must specify invoicing methodology to prevent disputes about payment timing.

### Change Orders and Scope Modifications in Lump Sum Contracts

The contract must establish clear procedures for handling scope changes. If the client requests services beyond the documented scope (additional building additions, significant aesthetic revisions, expanded site work), the architect should issue a change order documenting the additional scope and additional fee. The owner-architect agreement should establish the process for change order approval and fee adjustment.

Without clear change order procedures, the architect faces pressure to accommodate scope expansion within the fixed fee, either by stretching resources or accepting losses. Explicit scope definition and change order procedures protect both parties.

---

rows.title: Quasi Delict and Tort in Architectural Practice Civil Code Articles
rows.content:
## Quasi-Delict and Tort in Architectural Practice — Civil Code Articles 2176–2194

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define quasi-delict and culpa aquiliana under Civil Code Articles 2176–2194.
- Explain how quasi-delict applies to architectural malpractice.
- Distinguish contractual liability (Article 1723) from tort liability (Article 2176).
- Identify the elements of negligence an injured party must prove.

---
### Quasi-Delict Liability: The Foundation of Negligence-Based Claims

Civil Code Articles 2176–2194 establish the regime of _quasi-delict_ (culpa aquiliana), which allows recovery of damages based on negligence _independent of contract_. Article 2176 provides that _whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, is obliged to pay for the damage done_. This principle is broader than Article 1723's strict liability framework; quasi-delict requires proof of negligence but allows recovery for losses that do not rise to the level of structural collapse. For architects, quasi-delict liability applies when professional negligence causes injury or economic loss to clients, third parties, or neighboring property owners. Unlike Article 1723, quasi-delict claims are not limited to structural defects or building failures; they encompass design errors causing project delays, cost overruns, incomplete functionality, aesthetic defects, and environmental damage. The quasi-delict framework operates independently of contract terms and cannot be waived by service agreements.

### Negligence Elements and Professional Standard of Care

To establish quasi-delict liability, a claimant must prove four elements: (1) the architect owed a duty of care to the claimant; (2) the architect breached that duty through negligent act or omission; (3) the breach caused injury or loss; and (4) the claimant suffered quantifiable damages. The duty of care is measured against the _professional standard of care_—the degree of skill, diligence, and knowledge ordinarily exercised by licensed architects in the Philippines under similar circumstances. An architect who deviates from accepted professional practices, violates building codes, fails to consult specialists when necessary, or takes shortcuts in design analysis breaches this standard. Proof of negligence may come from expert testimony comparing the architect's conduct to professional norms, violation of applicable codes, failure to conduct required site investigations, or documented evidence of preventable errors. The burden of proof rests on the claimant, but once negligence is established, damages flow directly from that breach.

<ArticleMedia id="media-law012-negligence-elements" layout="single" variant="contained" type="image" status="placeholder" aspectRatio="4:3" title="Four Elements of Negligence in Quasi-Delict" alt="Diagram breaking down the four elements a claimant must prove: (1) Duty of Care, (2) Breach of Duty, (3) Causation, (4) Damages. Shows the professional standard of care benchmark and burden of proof on the claimant." placementIntent="legal-framework" suggestedSearchQuery="four elements of negligence quasi-delict Article 2176 architect Philippines" replacementNotes="Create a sequential four-box diagram. Box 1: Duty of Care (professional standard — what a competent architect would do). Arrow to Box 2: Breach (deviation from standard — code violations, inadequate investigation). Arrow to Box 3: Causation (breach directly caused injury/loss). Arrow to Box 4: Damages (quantifiable loss). Below: 'Burden of proof on claimant — expert testimony typically required.'" suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" alt="Four-element negligence proof: duty, breach, causation, damages" caption="Future diagram: four-element negligence proof: duty, breach, causation, damages" />

### Scope of Negligent Conduct Recoverable Under Quasi-Delict

Quasi-delict liability extends beyond structural failure to encompass: (1) design defects causing functional problems or safety hazards not amounting to collapse; (2) failure to comply with applicable building codes, zoning regulations, or environmental standards; (3) negligent site selection advice or inadequate geotechnical investigation; (4) design errors causing cost overruns or project delays; (5) failure to identify existing site conditions (contamination, hazards, encroachments); (6) inadequate coordination with structural, MEP, or specialty engineers; (7) negligent construction administration causing quality defects; and (8) failure to provide adequate or accurate project documentation. Architects may also face quasi-delict liability to third parties not their clients—neighboring property owners harmed by design defects affecting lateral support, environmental damage, drainage, or vibration transmission have standing to sue under quasi-delict even without privity of contract with the architect.

### Distinction Between Article 1723 and Quasi-Delict Liability

Article 1723 imposes liability for structural collapse within a **15-year window from the completion of the structure**, requiring the plaintiff to show a design or construction defect caused the collapse. By contrast, quasi-delict requires _proof of negligence_. However, quasi-delict is _broader in scope_ than Article 1723, covering defects and losses that do not cause collapse.

Additionally, quasi-delict claims face a different statute of limitations: under **Article 1146**, civil actions upon a quasi-delict must be instituted within _four (4) years_ from the day the quasi-delict is committed or the cause of action accrues. Conversely, actions based upon a written contract (culpa contractual) prescribe in 10 years under **Article 1144**. This four-year quasi-delict period differs from Article 1723, which dictates that actions must be brought within _10 years following the collapse of the building_ (provided the collapse happens within the 15-year liability window). An architect may face both Article 1723 liability (for structural defects) and quasi-delict liability (for negligence-based damages). The two frameworks are complementary, not mutually exclusive.

### Professional Standards and Good Faith Performance

Civil Code Article 2180 provides that architects are _responsible for damages caused by their employees' negligent acts_ performed in the course of work. This vicarious liability requires architects to maintain professional standards in recruiting, training, and supervising staff. Article 2189 holds employers/building owners liable for negligent acts of employees/contractors under their service; architects' liability for subcontracted professionals follows general quasi-delict principles (Art. 2176) and UAP SPP 206. Articles 2191–2194 further define rules for apportionment of liability when multiple parties contribute to injury or damage. These provisions create a framework where architects bear responsibility for the quality of all work delivered under their name, whether performed directly or through contracted professionals. Architects cannot disclaim liability for third-party errors by merely hiring specialists; they remain answerable to the client unless the client assumes the professional risk.

<LawCallout code="ra386" section="Articles 2176-2194 - Quasi-Delict">
Legal Basis: Civil Code of the Philippines, Articles 2176 (Quasi-Delict Definition), 2180 (Employer Liability), and 2194 (Solidary Liability). Quasi-delict covers negligence-based damages even without a contract.
</LawCallout>

Column 1: Article 1723 — Strict liability, structural collapse only, requires contractual relationship, 15-year exposure + 10-year post-collapse, solidary for construction defects. Column 2: Quasi-Delict (Art 2176-2194) — Negligence-based, any damage including non-collapse, applies without contract, 4-year prescription, third parties can sue. Column 3: Contractual (Art 1144) — Breach of written contract, 10-year prescription. Bottom section: 'Can proceed concurrently — not mutually exclusive.'" suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" alt="Four-element negligence proof: duty, breach, causation, damages" caption="Future diagram: four-element negligence proof: duty, breach, causation, damages" />

rows.title: Project Management in an Architectural Firm Scope Schedule Budget
rows.content:
## Project Management in an Architectural Firm—Scope, Schedule, Budget, and Communication Control

Project management is the discipline of planning, coordinating, and controlling project variables—scope, time, cost, and quality—to deliver projects successfully. Architects who manage projects well earn client loyalty, maintain profitability, and build reputation. Poor project management leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, scope disputes, and professional liability. This article addresses project management practices specific to architectural service delivery in the Philippines, governed by Republic Act No. 9266 and the Standards of Professional Practice.

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define project management within an architectural firm.
- Describe the four pillars: scope, schedule, budget, communication.
- Explain the architect's role as project manager vs. design lead.
- Identify project management tools and techniques relevant to practice.

### Project Scope Definition and Change Control

Under the UAP Standards of Professional Practice (SPP Documents 201-209), the scope of architectural services must be clearly defined to prevent disputes. A clear scope statement in the Owner-Architect Agreement outlines: (1) project phases (programming, schematic design, design development, contract documents, construction administration); (2) deliverables per phase (number of design options, presentation materials, construction document sets); (3) included services (site investigation, consultations, meetings); (4) excluded services (sustainability consulting, cost estimating, specialized engineering); and (5) client responsibilities (timely decisions, providing information).

The service agreement is the binding contract. Ambiguity about scope creates disputes—the client believes services are included; the architect believes they are additional and chargeable. Once scope is defined, any changes require formal change orders signed by both parties. Change orders should describe the additional work, explain the reason, and specify the additional fee or schedule impact.

Architects should resist scope creep—the gradual addition of services without compensation. Common scope creep includes: the client requesting a new design alternative during design development; asking for detailed cost estimating when not contracted; requesting ongoing consulting after project completion. Architects should politely but firmly direct these requests to change order procedures as mandated by SPP guidelines.

### Schedule Management and Milestone Tracking

Schedules establish expected completion dates for each project phase and identify dependencies. A typical architectural project takes 6–18 months from programming through construction documents, depending on project complexity and client decision speed. The architect should establish interim milestones—schematic design completion by date X, design development review by date Y—and communicate these clearly to the client.

Delays typically result from slow client decisions (approvals, information), design complexity requiring rework, or regulatory reviews (building permit, environmental approval). The architect cannot control all delays but should proactively identify bottlenecks and communicate the impact on the schedule. If environmental review takes 4 months (as required by regulatory agencies), the schedule should reflect this from the outset.

The architect should document when delays are client-caused (late decisions, delayed information) versus architect-caused (design rework). This documentation protects the architect if the final schedule is extended and the client claims the architect is responsible.

### Budget Management and Fee Collection

As outlined in SPP Document 202 (Regular Design Services), architects are typically compensated through standard methods such as: percentage of Project Construction Cost (PCC), Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses, Professional Fee Plus Expenses, Lump Sum or Fixed Fee, Per Diem/Honorarium, or Mixed Methods of Compensation.

Percentage fees align architect and client interests but require clear boundaries if the project scope expands. Lump-sum fees lock the architect's cost; if the project proves more complex, the architect absorbs cost overruns. The architect should track hours and costs throughout the project. If a lump-sum contract is used, monitoring actual hours against budgeted hours reveals whether the project is on financial track. If hours are exceeding budget, the architect can request a change order or discuss project scope adjustment.

Furthermore, Republic Act No. 9266 (The Architecture Act of 2004), specifically **Section 36 (Collection of Professional Fees)**, legally mandates and protects the registered and licensed architect's right to collect remuneration for services rendered. Fee collection discipline is essential to firm profitability. Invoices should be submitted promptly; payment terms should be stated in the contract (usually net 15 or 30 days). If a client delays payment, the architect should follow up promptly. Non-payment can damage firm cash flow and project morale.

### Communication Management: Meetings, Decisions, and Documentation

Clear communication prevents misunderstanding and protects the architect. The architect should: (1) document all design decisions and the rationale; (2) maintain meeting minutes summarizing decisions, action items, and responsible parties; (3) submit design and construction documents in clear, professional format; and (4) respond promptly to client inquiries.

Design decisions should be documented through sketches, memos, and presentation materials. If the client later claims a feature was not what they wanted, documentation showing the design decision was approved protects the architect. Meeting minutes should note attendees, topics discussed, decisions made, and next steps. Email correspondence confirming decisions creates a written record.

For virtual projects or remote teams, communication discipline is even more critical. Architects should use project collaboration platforms (shared document repositories, messaging systems) that maintain records and avoid information loss.

### Quality Control and Constructability Review

The architect must verify that construction documents are complete, coordinated, and compliant with codes and standards (such as the National Building Code of the Philippines). A constructability review—ideally with contractor input—helps identify build-ability issues, cost-saving opportunities, and construction sequence challenges. Rework during construction is costly and may extend the schedule.

Internal quality control processes include: design reviews by senior staff, code compliance checklists, consultant coordination reviews (MEP, structural, landscape integration), and final document review before issuance. These processes catch errors before they reach the client or the contractor.

<Tip>**Five essential quality control processes:** (1) design reviews by senior staff; (2) code compliance checklists; (3) consultant coordination reviews (MEP, structural, landscape); (4) final document review before issuance; (5) constructability review with contractor input. These catch errors before they reach the client or contractor.</Tip>

### Consultant Coordination and Agreement Management

Under RA 9266 and the SPP, the architect is the prime professional responsible for the overall design. Architects typically engage allied professionals and consultants (structural engineers, MEP engineers, landscape architects, specialty consultants).

Clear agreements with consultants must specify their scope, deliverables, coordination obligations, insurance requirements, and fee arrangements. The architect acts as the lead coordinator—ensuring consultants submit work on schedule, review each other's work for conflicts, and issue coordinated documents. Disputes among consultants (structural vs. MEP design conflicts, for example) are the architect's responsibility to manage and resolve through integrated design. The architect should establish clear coordination protocols, conduct regular design meetings, and use BIM or other coordination tools to catch conflicts early.

### Risk Management and Professional Liability

Project risks include: client default on payment, design errors causing construction cost overruns, regulatory disapproval delaying the project, and consultant errors. The architect should identify these risks early and develop mitigation strategies. Professional liability insurance protects against design errors; contract language should specify who bears risk for regulatory delays or client-initiated changes.

The architect must maintain complete project files including drawings, correspondence, meeting minutes, and design calculations. These files document the work performed and are essential if disputes arise or if a PRC Board of Architecture investigation occurs. Under the Civil Code of the Philippines (Article 1723), the architect holds a 15-year liability for the collapse of a building due to defects in plans or specifications.

### Post-Project Review and Continuous Improvement

After project completion, the architect should conduct a brief post-project review. Was the project completed on schedule? Within budget? Did the design meet the client's needs? What went well? What could improve? This reflection helps the firm learn and improve processes for future projects.

Client feedback, whether positive or critical, is valuable. A client survey or exit interview can identify areas for improvement. Firms that systematically review projects and implement improvements build strong reputations and attract repeat clients.

---



<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-prac-frm-019-project-manag-0" type="image" caption="Project Management in Architecture — Scope, Schedule, Budget, Communication Framework" description="Four-quadrant diagram showing project management areas in architectural practice: Scope (design phase deliverables, SOW management), Schedule (phase timeline, milestone tracking), Budget (fee monitoring, change order management), Communication (stakeholder updates, RFI process, meeting minutes). Center hub shows integration with SPP 202 phase deliverables." />

rows.title: Data Privacy Act RA 10173 the Architect's Obligations When Handling
rows.content:
## Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)—The Architect's Obligations When Handling Client Information

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Explain the architect's obligations under RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act).
- Describe how DPA applies to client information, project data, and employee records.
- Identify required data protection measures for architectural firms.
- Apply DPA compliance rules to practice scenarios.

### Scope of RA 10173: Personal Information Controllers and Processors

RA 10173 defines a _personal information controller_ (PIC) as an entity that decides the purpose and manner of processing personal data. A _personal information processor_ (PIP) is an entity that processes data on behalf of a PIC. In typical architectural practice, the client (owner or facility manager) is the PIC, and the architect may be a PIP if processing data at the client's direction.

However, architects sometimes act as PICs—for example, when maintaining a database of building occupants for emergency egress planning, or collecting tenant information for a mixed-use development. In both roles, architects have legal obligations to protect data and implement reasonable security measures.

### Key Obligations Under RA 10173

The law imposes several core obligations on PICs and PIPs. First, _transparency_: the data subject (occupant or tenant) must be informed what personal information is collected, why, and how it will be used. Second, _purpose limitation_: data collected for one purpose cannot be used for another without consent. Third, _data security_: the organization must implement reasonable measures to prevent unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction.

Fourth, _data retention_: personal information must not be kept longer than necessary for the stated purpose. Building emergency plans may require occupant lists; once the building is demolished or the tenant leaves, this data should be deleted. Fifth, _breach notification_: if personal data is compromised, the PIC must notify the National Privacy Commission and affected individuals without undue delay, as per NPC guidelines.

### Reasonable Security Measures Architects Must Implement

"Reasonable security" is not absolutely defined but requires measures proportionate to the sensitivity of the data and the risk of unauthorized access. For architects, reasonable measures include: (1) limiting access to sensitive project information to authorized personnel only; (2) encrypting digital files containing personal or confidential client information; (3) securing physical files in locked cabinets with restricted key access; (4) requiring confidentiality agreements from staff; (5) implementing access logs to track who accessed sensitive files; and (6) securely disposing of information when no longer needed (shredding paper, securely deleting digital files).

For BIM models containing detailed site and occupancy information, architects should restrict access to the project team, require login credentials, and avoid storing sensitive data on public cloud services without encryption. Client facility plans should not be posted on promotional websites without permission.

### Privacy Considerations in Project Delivery

When architects conduct site investigations, they may photograph occupants, measure occupied spaces, or document existing conditions that reveal operational information. Before collecting such data, architects should inform the client and document the client's consent. Design charrettes and programming sessions may elicit sensitive information about client operations, financial constraints, or strategic plans. This information is confidential and must not be disclosed to third parties or competitors.

During construction administration, architects may observe security weaknesses, occupancy patterns, or operational issues. While architects have a duty to report code violations or safety hazards, they should not disclose operational information that goes beyond what is necessary to address the specific issue. For example, identifying that a security camera placement is ineffective is relevant; disclosing the entire security system layout to unrelated parties is not.

### Duty to Implement Data Protection Officer Requirements

RA 10173 requires designation of an individual(s) accountable for compliance; large architectural firms processing significant personal data should assess if a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is required per NPC guidelines. The DPO oversees data protection compliance, fields privacy complaints, and ensures the organization meets legal obligations. Firms should assess whether they process large-scale data or sensitive information of occupants, tenants, employees, or building users. If so, appointing a DPO (internal or external) demonstrates legal compliance and professional responsibility.

### Client Information and Intellectual Property Rights

Architects must distinguish between intellectual property in the design (which the architect typically retains copyright to) and the client's confidential business information. The client's operational data, financial information, and facility requirements are the client's property. The architect's copyright extends to the design expression (plans, drawings, specifications) but not to the underlying information the client provided.

Service agreements should clarify: (1) what project information is confidential; (2) what use the architect may make of project information for professional development, case studies, or awards submissions; (3) whether the architect may photograph or publicize the finished building; and (4) under what circumstances the architect may share project information with consultants, contractors, or third parties.

### Enforcement and Penalties

The National Privacy Commission (NPC) enforces RA 10173. Violations can result in administrative fines, orders to cease processing, and directives to delete unlawfully held data. In extreme cases, criminal penalties apply for willful and malicious processing. A data breach that the architect fails to report can expose the architect and the firm to liability both to the NPC and to affected individuals.

Professional disciplinary bodies (Board of Architecture) may also view serious privacy violations as grounds for disciplinary action under the Code of Ethical Conduct. An architect who negligently disclosed a client's confidential information or failed to protect data adequately could face complaints alleging breach of professional ethics.

### Practical Compliance Checklist for Architects

Architects should implement the following: (1) maintain a data inventory documenting what personal information is collected, why, and how long it is retained; (2) draft privacy notices to inform data subjects; (3) obtain written consent before collecting sensitive data; (4) implement confidentiality agreements with staff; (5) encrypt sensitive files; (6) restrict access to authorized personnel only; (7) maintain audit trails; (8) secure disposal of information when no longer needed; (9) have a breach response plan; and (10) provide staff training on data protection obligations.

<LawCallout code="ra10173" section="Section 11 - Security of Personal Information">
Legal Basis: RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act of 2012). Architects collecting/processing client personal data are 'personal information controllers' subject to NPC (National Privacy Commission) oversight.
</LawCallout>

## Phase 3: Contract Documents: Working Drawings, Specifications, and the 50% Fee
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

- Describe the deliverables of the Contract Document Phase (Phase 4): working drawings, technical specifications, and bidding documents.
- Explain why this phase earns 50% of the total design services fee under SPP 202.
- Identify the components of a complete contract document package and their roles in construction administration.
- Apply Contract Document Phase requirements to LEA scenarios involving document completeness, specification types, and bid package assembly.

The Contract Document Phase represents the most significant single payment under SPP 202, earning 50% of the architect's total design services fees. This phase produces the comprehensive drawings and specifications needed to communicate all construction requirements to contractors and building officials.

<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-prac-svc-007-phase-3-contract-docume" type="image" caption="SPP Doc 202 Six-Phase Framework — Contract Documents Phase in Context" description="Process flow highlighting Phase 4 (Contract Documents) within the six-phase SPP Doc 202 framework: Project Definition → Schematic Design → Design Development → Contract Documents (50% fee, working drawings, technical specifications, bidding documents, permit filings) → Bidding → Construction Admin." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

### Contract Document Deliverables

<KeyValues pairs={[["SPP Document", "201 (Pre-Design), 202 (Regular Design), 203 (Specialized)"], ["Compensation", "MDPE, Lump Sum, Per Diem, Professional Fee + Expenses"], ["Fee Basis", "Percentage of PCC or MDPE"]]} />
Based on approved Design Development documents, the architect prepares complete Contract Documents consisting of detailed designs and construction drawings setting forth in detail all work required for architectural, structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, sanitary, electronic, and communications systems. Technical Specifications describing type and quality of materials, finish, manner of construction, and general conditions under which construction will occur are prepared comprehensively. The architect submits seven sets of all construction drawings and technical specifications for purposes of obtaining building permits.

### Coordination, Cost Updates, and Government Filings

<KeyValues pairs={[["SPP Document", "201 (Pre-Design), 202 (Regular Design), 203 (Specialized)"], ["Compensation", "MDPE, Lump Sum, Per Diem, Professional Fee + Expenses"], ["Fee Basis", "Percentage of PCC or MDPE"]]} />

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Expect scenario-based questions where you must determine which phase a specific deliverable belongs to. Key percentages to memorize: Schematic Design (15%), Design Development (35%), Contract Documents (50%).</ExamTip>
Contract Documents require extensive coordination among all design disciplines to ensure completeness and consistency. The architect updates the Statement of Probable Project Construction Cost based on changes in scope, requirements, or market conditions. The architect also assists the owner in filing required documents to secure approval from government authorities having jurisdiction over the design of the project. This comprehensive support during permitting represents a critical service ensuring regulatory compliance.

<ExamTip>**LEA Pattern:** Expect scenario-based questions where you must determine which phase a specific deliverable belongs to. Key percentages to memorize: Schematic Design (15%), Design Development (35%), Contract Documents (50%).</ExamTip>
### Fee Significance and Cumulative Achievement

<ProcessFlow steps={["Identify client needs", "Define scope of services", "Prepare proposal/contract", "Execute pre-design activities", "Deliver phase outputs", "Submit for owner approval"]} />

<ProcessFlow steps={["Identify client needs", "Define scope of services", "Prepare proposal/contract", "Execute pre-design activities", "Deliver phase outputs", "Submit for owner approval"]} />

Upon completion of Contract Documents, the architect has earned 50% of total design fees. The 50% payment for this phase (cumulative 50% of total design fees) reflects the substantial technical work, coordination effort, and responsibility for accuracy in these construction documents. This largest single phase payment represents the architect's acknowledgment of the critical nature of accurate, complete contract documents that form the basis for all construction work and legal disputes. Students often underestimate this phase's importance compared to earlier conceptual work.

rows.title: Ecological considerations in site planning
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Analyze ecological site conditions — watershed hydrology, biodiversity, geological hazards, vegetation — and apply findings to site planning decisions, identify PD 1067 water body easements, and integrate ecological constraints with development programming.

Ecological considerations in site planning address water, biodiversity, environmental hazards, and the living systems that surround and integrate with human settlement. This is not environmental law (that belongs to other articles)—this is what a site planner needs to understand about the natural conditions on a site and how those conditions constrain or enable development.

### Watershed and Hydrology

Every site sits within a watershed—the land area that drains to a particular stream, river, or coastal area. Understanding the watershed tells you where water comes from and where it goes.

**Key Concepts**

1. **Drainage patterns** — Water flows downslope along predictable paths. On a site with contours, you can see drainage direction: water flows perpendicular to contour lines, downslope.

2. **Groundwater and aquifers** — Underground water stored in soil and rock layers. The water table is the depth where groundwater begins. Sites with high water tables require special foundation design.

3. **Stormwater runoff** — When rain falls, it either infiltrates soil, flows overland, or evaporates. Impervious surfaces (pavement, roofs) increase runoff and reduce infiltration. Steep slopes increase runoff velocity.

4. **Water balance** — Inputs (rainfall, groundwater inflow) minus outputs (evapotranspiration, runoff, deep percolation) determine whether a site is wet or dry seasonally.

**Site Planning Implications**
- Sites in upper watershed areas have minimal inflow and depend on rainfall
- Mid-watershed sites collect runoff from upslope and generate runoff to downslope neighbors
- Lower watershed sites (near rivers or coast) receive upstream flows and must plan for flooding
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-004-02-what-you-need-to-know-fo" type="image" caption="Watershed and Hydrology — Site Drainage Patterns Diagram" description="Cross-sectional diagram of a watershed showing three zones: upper watershed (rainfall-dependent, minimal inflow), mid-watershed (collects runoff from upslope, generates runoff downslope), and lower watershed (near river/coast, receives upstream flows, flood-prone). Annotated with stormwater runoff arrows, groundwater table, impervious surface infiltration, and PD 1067 water body easements (3m/20m/40m)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

### Flood Zones and Flood Risk

Flooding occurs when water exceeds the channel capacity of rivers, esteros (streams), or the drainage system.

**Flood-Prone Areas in the Philippines**

Metro Manila and coastal cities frequently flood because:
- High water tables and sea level proximity
- Inadequate estero and drainage infrastructure
- Upstream watershed degradation increases runoff
- Typhoons bring intense rainfall (300+ mm in 24 hours)
- Storm surge combines with high tides in coastal areas

**What Site Planners Document**

1. **Historical flood elevation** — Using flood records or witness accounts, determine how high water has reached during past typhoons or heavy rains
2. **Flood return period** — 5-year, 10-year, 25-year flood elevations help assess risk. A site flooded in a 5-year event is riskier than one flooded only in a 25-year event
3. **Flood source** — Is flooding from river overflow, storm surge, inadequate drainage, or groundwater rise?
4. **Site elevation relative to historical flood marks** — If the site is below historical flood levels, development requires flood-proofing strategies

**Design Responses**
- Elevate sensitive uses (housing, offices) above the 25-year flood level
- Use ground floors for parking or flood-resilient storage (not housing)
- Install flood barriers or closures
- Maintain or restore wetlands and detention areas for natural flood absorption
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-004-02-what-you-need-to-know-fo" type="image" caption="Flood Risk Assessment — Return Period and Site Elevation Diagram" description="Cross-section diagram showing flood return periods (5-year, 10-year, 25-year flood elevations) relative to site elevation. Design responses illustrated: elevating sensitive uses above 25-year flood level, using ground floors for flood-resilient storage, maintaining wetlands for natural flood absorption. Philippine context: Metro Manila high water table, inadequate estero drainage, typhoon rainfall intensity." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

### Wetlands and Water Bodies

Wetlands are permanently or seasonally inundated areas—mangroves, marshes, fishponds, rice paddies. They are among the most productive ecosystems.

**Why Wetlands Matter for Site Planning**

1. **Flood buffering** — Wetlands absorb and slowly release floodwater, reducing downstream flooding
2. **Biodiversity** — Fish, crustaceans, birds, and plants depend on wetlands for survival
3. **Water purification** — Wetlands filter sediment and absorb excess nutrients
4. **Livelihoods** — Wetland-dependent communities (fishers, rice farmers) depend on these areas for survival

**Water Body Easements (Referenced, Not Fully Taught Here)**

PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines) establishes mandatory easements from water bodies:
- **3 meters** from rivers/streams less than 3 meters wide
- **20 meters** from rivers/streams 3-20 meters wide
- **40 meters** from rivers/streams over 20 meters wide or navigable, and from lake shores/seas

These easements are no-build zones for permanent structures. Full treatment of PD 1067 and its application belongs to LEA-PLAN-005-03.

### Biodiversity and Habitat

A site may support native species—birds, fish, insects, plants. Development often fragments or destroys habitat.

**What Site Planners Assess**

1. **Vegetation types** — Are there native trees, secondary growth, or introduced/invasive species? What ecological role do they play?
2. **Fauna** — What birds, fish, mammals, or insects use the site? Are any threatened or endemic?
3. **Habitat connectivity** — Is the site isolated or does it connect to larger protected areas or corridors?
4. **Protected species** — The site or adjacent areas may be home to species protected by law (e.g., Philippine eagle, tarsier)

**Design Considerations**
- Preserve native vegetation where possible
- Create green corridors and stepping stones for wildlife movement
- Restore degraded areas with native species
- Manage exotic invasive species (water hyacinth, calamansi that escapes)

### Slope Stability and Landslide Risk

Steep, unstable slopes are hazardous.

**Indicators of Slope Instability**

1. **Soil composition** — Clay-rich soils are less stable than well-compacted sands; volcanic soils can collapse if saturated
2. **Slope angle** — Slopes steeper than 35–45° (depending on soil) are prone to slides
3. **Groundwater seepage** — Water emerging from a hillside indicates saturation; wet slopes are unstable
4. **Scarps and evidence of past movement** — Curved tree trunks, tilted utilities, bare soil patches, or tension cracks indicate previous slides
5. **Vegetation loss** — Areas recently deforested are highly prone to slides

**Site Planning Response**
- Do not build on slopes showing active instability indicators
- If development occurs, install slope stabilization (terracing, retaining walls, drainage)
- Maintain forest cover to bind soil
- Avoid removing vegetation from saturated slopes

### Soil and Geotechnical Conditions

Soil type, depth, and compaction affect buildability and foundation costs.

**Soil Classification**
- **Clay** — Fine particles; low permeability; compressible if soft; stable if properly compacted
- **Silt** — Between clay and sand; variable stability
- **Sand** — Larger particles; permeable; stable when compacted; liquefiable if saturated and shaken
- **Gravel** — Large particles; stable; good bearing capacity

**Geotechnical Risk in Philippine Sites**

1. **Soft clay in Metro Manila** — Deep soft clay layers require piles or special foundations; settlement risk is high
2. **Volcanic soils in Luzon** — Pumice and ash layers can be unstable when saturated; caves and voids are common
3. **Liquefaction near coasts** — Saturated sand near the water table can lose strength during earthquakes
4. **Buried obstacles** — Old foundations, debris, utilities, or unexploded ordnance (in WWII sites) may complicate excavation

**Site Planning Implications**
- A geotechnical investigation (test boring, soil lab analysis) is essential before design
- Poor soils increase foundation costs; consider site suitability before zoning or approving projects
- Avoid development on sites with unresolved geotechnical hazards

### Air Quality and Microclimate

Urban sites experience different air quality and temperature than rural areas.

**Urban Heat Island**
- Pavement and buildings absorb heat; vegetation is reduced
- Urban areas are 2–5°C warmer than surrounding rural areas
- Air stagnates over cities, trapping pollution

**Site Planning Mitigation**
- Increase tree canopy and vegetation
- Use lighter-colored pavement and roofing to reduce heat absorption
- Maintain ventilation corridors (gaps between buildings) for air flow
- Avoid blocking prevailing winds with dense built form

### Seismic and Geological Hazards

The Philippines sits on the Ring of Fire and experiences frequent earthquakes. Some sites are at higher risk than others.

**Fault Lines and PHIVOLCS Setbacks**

Active fault traces require setbacks. Structures must be at least **10 meters** from both sides of active fault traces (per PHIVOLCS/NBCP guidelines). Sites straddling a fault are unsuitable for habitation.

**Liquefaction Hazard**
- Saturated sand and silt near the water table may liquefy in earthquakes
- Coastal and low-lying sites are at higher risk
- Liquefaction reduces bearing capacity and causes differential settlement
- Design response: deeper piles, improved soil, or avoidance

**Tsunami and Storm Surge Risk**

Coastal sites are vulnerable to tsunami and typhoon storm surge.

**Post-Typhoon Yolanda Framework**: A **40-meter no-build zone** from mean high tide was established in select high-risk coastal municipalities (NDRP post-Yolanda, 2014). This restricts development in the immediate coastal strip, prioritizing evacuation space and reducing casualty risk.

### Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and ECC

Sites classified as Environmentally Critical Projects (ECPs) or located in Environmentally Critical Areas (ECAs) require an **Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC)** issued by DENR (Department of Environment and Natural Resources, not DHSUD).

**Reference Note**: Full treatment of PD 1586 (Philippine Environmental Impact Statement System) and ECC requirements belongs to LEA-PLAN-005-03. In this article, the planner notes: _"If the site is in an ECA or the project is an ECP, an EIA and ECC will be required."_ That is the extent of ecological site planning's role.

**Ecological Site Planning Does Not**
- Conduct the full EIA (that is DENR's role)
- Determine ECC requirements (that is DENR's determination)
- Prepare environmental compliance documents (that belongs to environmental specialists)

**What Site Planning Does**
- Identify if the site is in or near sensitive ecological areas
- Note whether ecological constraints exist
- Flag that further environmental assessment is needed

### What This Article Does NOT Own

- **Full treatment of PD 1067 easement law and enforcement** — LEA-PLAN-005-03
- **Full treatment of PD 1586 EIA and ECC issuance** — LEA-PLAN-005-03
- **Biodiversity surveys and species inventories** — Environmental specialists (outside LEA-PLAN)
- **Detailed hydrologic modeling** — Engineers (outside LEA-PLAN scope)
- **Design charrette and community ecological input** — LEA-PLAN-008-04
- **Ecological zone management after development** — LEA-PLAN-004-04

### Ecological Site Planning Checklist

<Tip>When analyzing a site's ecological conditions:

1. Map the watershed and identify drainage patterns
2. Check historical flood records and assess flood risk
3. Document existing wetlands, water bodies, and vegetation
4. Identify any protected or vulnerable species
5. Assess slope stability indicators and landslide risk
6. Review soil conditions and geotechnical constraints
7. Note proximity to active fault lines (PHIVOLCS)
8. Check if site is in an ECA or if project is an ECP (triggers EIA/ECC need)
9. Evaluate air quality and heat island effects
10. Document all constraints and inform preliminary site planning strategy

These inform feasibility; management and design choices come later.</Tip>

---

_LEA-PLAN-004-02: Ecological Considerations_
_Site Planning Series | Content Owner: Ecological Site Analysis and Environmental Constraints_
